explanations.explanation: Mark tells us right in the verse that Preparation Day is the day before the Sabbath. So the evening sky is a hint that the Sabbath is close. Joseph of Arimathea, a Council member, is about to act on that same evening. The writer wants us to see the timing, so I'm pointing at it too.

Mark says it plainly: Preparation Day is "the day before the Sabbath." So it isn't the day after or the day of. It's the day right before. Easy one to mix up, friend, because I've gotten weekends tangled up before, and I run the whole bakery schedule.

Mark says Joseph of Arimathea "boldly went to Pilate." Pilate is the governor, and Joseph is walking up to ask for the body of a man who was just crucified. I think that takes nerve. I'd rehearse that walk all the way there and still open with a comment about the weather.

The text says Joseph "boldly went to Pilate." Nothing in the verse shows him sneaking or hanging back. He's a prominent Council member who was waiting for the kingdom of God, and he walks right up. I think that's a man who steps forward when it counts.

Joseph asks Pilate for the body of Jesus. That's the whole request. Pilate then checks that Jesus is already dead, and afterward he grants the body to Joseph. Everything that happens next at the tomb hangs on this one ask.

The garments come up earlier, at the cross, where the soldiers divided them up and cast lots (Mark 15:24). Joseph isn't there for clothes. He walks in and asks for the body of Jesus. That's the request Pilate looks into.
Joseph doesn't ask for guards. In Mark's account, he asks Pilate for the body of Jesus, and that's all. Then he buys linen and does the burying himself. No guard shows up anywhere in this passage.

Pilate summons the centurion to ask if Jesus is really already dead. The centurion is the one who can answer, and Pilate confirms it with him. Only after that does Pilate grant the body to Joseph. Pilate was surprised, and he double-checked before he decided anything.

Pilate doesn't call for the high priest here. The text says he summons the centurion. That's who he asks, and that's who confirms it. Pilate gets his answer from the centurion before he does anything else.

A tetrarch is a ruler over a part of a region, and Luke 3:1 names Herod as tetrarch of Galilee. But Pilate doesn't summon one in this scene. Mark says he summons the centurion to ask if Jesus is already dead. Wrong rank, friend, but I'd have panicked at the titles too.
It goes the other way. Once Pilate confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. He didn't refuse. The surprise at Jesus already being dead ended with a yes.
Right, friend. Mark says that when Pilate had confirmed it with the centurion, he granted the body to Joseph. So the answer was yes. The check was just Pilate making sure first.

explanations.answer: A tomb cut out of rock
explanations.explanation: Joseph places the body in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. He had wrapped it in linen first. Then he rolled a stone against the entrance. The place matters later, because the women will walk back to it.

explanations.answer: A plot in the potter's field
explanations.explanation: The potter's field does show up in the Bible. Matthew 27:7 says it was bought as a burial place for foreigners. But that's not where Joseph lays Jesus. Mark says he placed the body in a tomb cut out of the rock.

explanations.answer: A grave under an oak tree
explanations.explanation: No oak tree in this scene, friend. Mark says Joseph placed the body in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. That's a built space with an entrance, and it has a stone for a door. The text doesn't mention any tree.

Joseph rolled a stone against the entrance to the tomb. Later, Mark tells us this stone was extremely large. So keep it in mind, because it matters in the next stop. A door that size doesn't move without help.
A log would be a pretty small door for a tomb. Mark says Joseph rolled a stone against the entrance. And later the text calls that stone extremely large. Rolling it is the whole point of the verse.
Mark doesn't mention a beam. The text says Joseph rolled a stone against the entrance. Things get rolled, not propped up, in this verse. The stone is what the women will ask about later.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed. They're paying attention to the spot. I think that's a heavy moment, and they stay for it anyway. They won't forget that place.
No soldiers show up here in Mark. The two Marys saw where His body was placed. That's the detail the text gives us. Nothing in these verses says anyone stood guard.

Pilate stays out of this scene. He already granted the body to Joseph, and that's the last we see of him in this passage. The two Marys saw where His body was placed. The tomb scene belongs to Joseph and the women.

They bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. The Sabbath is over, so they can finally go. Those spices tell us what they expect to find. They expect to find Jesus' body, and that's it.
Guarding isn't what the spices are for. Mark says they bought them so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. Spices are for anointing, friend. Nobody ever guarded a tomb with cinnamon.

Carrying isn't the plan here. The women bought spices so they could go and anoint the body of Jesus. The body is already in the tomb, so they're heading there with spices in hand. Anointing is the job.

explanations.answer: Who will roll away the stone
explanations.explanation: They were asking one another, "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?" They're thinking about a very big stone. Nobody in the group has an answer yet. I think they're just working through the problem as they walk.

Soldiers aren't on their minds in Mark's account. The women ask, "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?" That's a practical worry about getting inside. The text doesn't mention soldiers anywhere near here.

They already know which tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joseph saw where His body was placed (Mark 15:47). So the question on the road is about the stone: "Who will roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb?" They know where to go. They just don't know how to get in.
It's the opposite. Mark says that when they looked up, the stone had been rolled away. It was extremely large, and it was moved anyway. Their question on the road already had an answer.
Yes, friend. When the women looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away. Mark adds that it was extremely large. The very thing they were asking about was already open.

explanations.answer: A young man in a white robe
explanations.explanation: They entered the tomb and saw a young man dressed in a white robe, sitting on the right side. Mark doesn't give his name. So I'll call him what the text calls him. The women didn't expect anyone to be in there.
Joseph's linen was the cloth he bought to wrap the body (Mark 15:46). He isn't sitting in the tomb. The women see a young man dressed in a white robe, on the right side. Same linen idea, wrong guy.
There's no armor in this scene. Mark says the women saw a young man dressed in a white robe, sitting on the right side. A robe, not a uniform. And the text doesn't call him a soldier.

Mark says they were alarmed. They walked into a tomb expecting one thing and found a young man in a white robe sitting there. The young man answers that right away with, "Do not be alarmed." I'd have been alarmed too, friend.
Relief isn't what Mark says. He says they were alarmed. The young man then tells them, "Do not be alarmed." You only say that to people who are already alarmed.
Delight hasn't hit yet. Mark says that when the women saw him, they were alarmed. Then the young man says, "Do not be alarmed." The good news is about to come, but they aren't there yet.

explanations.answer: He has risen and is not here
explanations.explanation: The young man says, "He has risen! He is not here!" Then he points to the place where they put Him. The tomb is empty because Jesus has risen. That's the heart of this whole passage.

explanations.answer: He was moved to another tomb
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say that. The young man says, "He has risen! He is not here!" Nobody moved the body, according to what he tells them. He says Jesus has risen.
That isn't what the young man says. He says, "He has risen! He is not here!" He doesn't mention Pilate or soldiers at all. The message is that Jesus has risen.
The young man tells them to go and tell His disciples and Peter. Peter gets named on his own. The message says Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee. The women are handed a job.
Pilate and the centurion were in the burial scene earlier. But the message isn't for them. The young man says, "go, tell His disciples and Peter." That's the list.
The chief priests and scribes aren't who he names. The young man says to go and tell His disciples and Peter. The message is for the people who followed Jesus. The text names nobody else.

The message says, "He is going ahead of you into Galilee." Galilee is the region in the north where Jesus did much of His teaching. The young man adds, "There you will see Him." The disciples are given a place to go.
Bethany is a village near Jerusalem, and Mark 11:1 mentions it. But the young man doesn't send the disciples there. He says Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee. That's where they'll see Him.
Emmaus is a village that shows up in Luke 24:13. It isn't in the message here. The young man says Jesus is going ahead of the disciples into Galilee. Wrong road, friend.

The young man says, "There you will see Him, just as He told you." That "just as He told you" means Jesus had already said it. So the disciples aren't hearing about Galilee for the first time. The women are passing along a promise that was already made.
The young man ends the message with, "just as He told you." So Jesus had already told them. The women are delivering a reminder with a very big update attached.
Mark says the opposite. In their fear they did not say a word to anyone. They left the tomb and ran away, trembling and bewildered. Nobody on the road heard anything from them.
Right, friend. Mark says that in their fear they did not say a word to anyone. They ran from the tomb trembling and bewildered. I think that tells you how big that morning felt.
